opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to be honest with ourselves about what "commercially viable" actually means in robotics right now. There's a lot of excitement in the field, a lot of beautiful demos, but a demo is not a business. So the way I'd want us to organize is around a few principles.

First, start from a real, narrow use case where a customer is already feeling pain and will pay today, not in five years. It's tempting to say "we're building a general-purpose robot," and long term, maybe that's the dream. But if you try to solve everything at once, you end up solving nothing well enough for someone to sign a contract. So you pick a scenario, whether it's a particular kind of manipulation task, a logistics step, or an inspection job, and you go deep. You learn what reliability the customer actually needs, what the cost ceiling is, what the deployment environment really looks like, which is never what it looked like in the lab.

Second, the team structure has to close the loop between research and deployment. In a lot of robotics companies, the algorithm people sit in one place, the hardware people in another, and the field engineers are off at customer sites, and the information doesn't flow back. I'd want small, cross-functional groups where the people training the models are also seeing the failure cases from real deployments every week. In robotics, data from the real world is the most valuable asset you have, and the organization should be built so that every deployment makes the system better.

Third, be disciplined about the hardware-software balance. Hardware is expensive, slow to iterate, and it's where a lot of startups burn their money. So you want hardware that's good enough and cost-effective, and you put a lot of the differentiation into software and learning, things that scale and improve over time without a new production run. But you can't ignore hardware either, because if the robot isn't robust, no algorithm will save you at a customer site.

And finally, culturally, I think we need to combine ambition with patience. Robotics is a long game. You need people who believe in the big vision, embodied intelligence that's genuinely useful in everyday life, but who are also willing to do the unglamorous work: debugging a gripper at two in the morning, sitting with a customer to understand why their workflow is different from what we assumed. If we can keep both of those things alive at the same time, the long-term vision and the near-term commercial grounding, then I think we have a real chance to build something that lasts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing hardware and software, but it does not mention VLA capabilities or say they require resources comparable to robotics hardware.

r002.rationale: The response does not address investment-funded companies’ ability to develop hardware and VLA capabilities simultaneously.

r003.rationale: It proposes cross-functional teams within one company, not collaboration among companies specializing in different parts of robotics development.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most robotics companies fail not because the technology isn't impressive, but because they try to do everything at once. So if I were organizing Miaodong's efforts, I'd start by being very disciplined about one thing: pick a single scenario where a robot clearly saves someone money or solves a pain they already pay to solve, and go deep there before going wide.

That means the organization shouldn't be structured around "humanoid" or "general intelligence" as the north star in the near term. Those are great long-term directions, but commercially they're a trap if you lead with them. Instead I'd organize around a vertical team that owns a real customer end to end: the hardware, the software, the deployment, the maintenance, and most importantly the unit economics. That team should know exactly what a customer pays today, what the robot costs to build and operate, and what the payback period is. If that number isn't under roughly two years, you don't have a product yet, you have a demo.

Second, I'd separate the platform work from the application work. There's a core that's reusable: perception, manipulation, the data pipeline, the control stack, the hardware modules. That should be a platform group whose customer is the internal vertical teams, not the outside world. The mistake many companies make is letting the platform group define the product. The vertical team should pull from the platform, and the platform should be measured by how fast it lets a new scenario go from zero to deployable.

Third, data and deployment have to be treated as a first-class business function, not an afterthought. Every robot in the field is a data collection device, and the company that closes the loop fastest between field failures and model updates wins. So I'd put real investment into operations: field engineers, remote monitoring, a teleoperation fallback so a robot that gets stuck doesn't become a lost customer. It's unglamorous, but it's what makes the second hundred units cheaper than the first ten.

Fourth, on supply chain and hardware, China has an enormous advantage, and Miaodong should lean on it. Don't over-engineer custom components early. Use what the ecosystem already produces at scale, standardize the interfaces, and only build custom where it actually differentiates. Cost is a feature in robotics. A robot that's eighty percent as capable at forty percent of the price wins in most commercial settings.

And finally, the organization needs a clear owner for the commercial side who has equal standing with the technical leadership. Too many robotics companies are run entirely by engineers who assume demand will appear once the product is good enough. It won't. You need someone whose whole job is sitting with factory managers or logistics operators or whoever the customer is, understanding their workflow, and feeding that back into the roadmap.

So in short: one vertical, owned end to end, with real unit economics; a platform team serving those verticals rather than driving them; operations and data as a core function; ruthless cost discipline on hardware; and commercial leadership at the table from day one. Do that well, and the broader ambitions, the general-purpose stuff, become something you can fund from revenue instead of just hoping investors keep believing.

r003.rationale: The response proposes organizing internal vertical and platform teams, not collaboration among separate companies specializing in different parts of robotics development.

astra-6.text:
I think Miaodong Technology should organize around a specific customer problem, with a clear path from technical development to deployment and revenue. Where can a robot do useful work reliably, and where is that work valuable enough that a customer will pay for it?

I would start with one relatively narrow application. Put engineering, product, sales, and deployment people together around that application, so they share responsibility for the outcome. The engineers need to understand what happens at the customer’s site, and the commercial team needs to understand what the technology can actually deliver.

Then measure the whole business case: reliability, installation time, maintenance, support, and the customer’s payback period. A successful demonstration is encouraging, but the real test is whether you can deploy the next ten robots without ten separate engineering projects.

Once that works, you can build shared technology and expand into adjacent applications. My priority would be to establish a repeatable business in one market, then use what you learn to guide the broader robotics effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Miaodong Technology should start with a very concrete question: what job can a robot do for a customer who is willing to pay for it? Then organize the company around delivering that outcome.

That means choosing a focused application and bringing engineering, product, sales, and deployment together around it. The team needs to understand the customer’s workflow, what performance is required, and whether the economics work after installation, maintenance, and support—not just whether the robot can perform a task in a demonstration.

I would start with a small number of customers, learn from actual use, and turn those lessons into a repeatable product. Custom projects can help you learn, but if every deployment requires a new engineering effort, it becomes difficult to scale. The priority should be to establish one commercially sound application, then expand from that foundation.
